title: The comparison report is slow or lagging: where to look, in order
content:
This is one of the three symptoms the founder named. Work it in this order, because the cheap checks eliminate most of the causes and the expensive one is last.

FIRST, establish that it is slow rather than absent. A report that never appears is a different fault with a different investigation -- check whether the comparison function produced a run record at all for that inquiry. Remember that the run record is written at the END of the work, so a timeout or a crash writes NOTHING, and absence is evidence of failure rather than of quiet.

SECOND, measure it instead of believing the report. There is no duration column anywhere: compute elapsed time from the run record's start and finish timestamps for the comparison function, grouped by day and by inquiry, and get an actual distribution. Slow compared to what is a real question -- a first-ever comparison for an inquiry with many quotes is legitimately slower than a small one, so break it down by quote count before concluding.

THIRD, and this is the highest-yield check by a wide margin: the comparison cache holds zero rows and has never held any. The function reads it and upserts to it, and its own log line records that the write did not happen, so every re-open re-runs the model at full cost rather than returning a cached analysis. If the complaint is that the report is slow the SECOND time it is opened, that is the cause, and it is a defect in the cache write rather than in the comparison itself. Confirm by checking whether the cache has gained a row since; if it is still empty after a comparison ran, the write is failing silently.

FOURTH, check the wall-clock budget. The function subtracts elapsed time from a fixed limit and passes the remainder downstream as a client timeout. As total time rises, the budget handed to the model shrinks, so a slow early phase makes the later phase more likely to fail or to fall back. That budget is never persisted, so it has to be reasoned about from the code and the elapsed time rather than read.

FIFTH, only now consider the model path. There is a deterministic fallback module used when every paid attempt fails; a comparison that came back from the fallback will look different and may be blamed for feeling wrong rather than slow. Under the standing hold on paid routes the fallback is the expected path, and a report produced deterministically is correct behaviour, not a degradation to escalate.

WHAT NOT TO DO: do not go looking at the two comparison report tables. Both are empty and neither is called by the live function; they are finished capability with no entry point and have nothing to say about a live slowness.

structured_data.symptom: the generated comparison report is lagging

order.check: slow or absent -- is there a run record at all; absence means failure, because the record is written at the end
compute elapsed time from the run record start and finish timestamps; no duration column exists; break down by quote count
the comparison cache holds zero rows and has never held any; the write fails silently, so every re-open recomputes at full cost -- highest yield check
the wall-clock budget shrinks as elapsed time rises and is passed downstream as a client timeout; never persisted, reason from the code
the deterministic fallback -- under the paid-route hold this is the expected path and is not a degradation

structured_data.do_not: investigate the two comparison report tables; both are empty and unreferenced by the live function

title: Registration is failing for one customer but not others: how to separate the four different faults
content:
This is one of the three symptoms the founder named, and the first move is to refuse the framing. Registration is not one step and there is no registration function. A complaint that registration failed can mean four unrelated things, in three different functions, and reading code before establishing which one wastes the investigation.

THE FOUR. One, the sign-in code never arrived -- a messaging or suppression fault, nothing to do with account creation. Two, the code arrived and verification failed -- an expiry, a mismatch, or a rate limit. Three, verification succeeded but no customer row appeared -- an account-creation fault. Four, the account exists and a LATER step refuses because the profile is incomplete, which surfaces as a precondition-required response carrying an explicit list of what is missing, and is correct behaviour rather than a bug.

HOW TO TELL THEM APART, cheapest first. Does an authentication user exist for that email? If yes, verification succeeded and you are in case three or four. Does a customer row exist? If yes, you are in case four and the answer is the missing list, not a defect. If no user exists, check the verification records and the suppression list for that address before anything else -- a suppressed address produces a perfect silence that looks exactly like a broken system.

WHY ONE CUSTOMER AND NOT OTHERS is itself the strongest clue, and it points away from code. Code paths do not usually discriminate between users; DATA about a user does. The things that are per-address and therefore explain a single-user failure: suppression, a stale verification record, a rate limit already consumed, an existing row in an unexpected state, an address that differs by case or whitespace from the one being looked up, and a phone-only attempt -- which is refused outright with a message to sign up by email, before any messaging charge, and is easily reported as registration is broken.

THE STRUCTURAL DEFECT WORTH KNOWING. The customer email column carries no unique index, so account creation cannot be an upsert: it updates by email and inserts only if no row was updated. Two verifications racing for the same address can therefore both find nothing to update and both insert, producing two customer rows for one identity. That is not a hypothetical shape -- it is what the absence of a unique index means. If a single user is behaving inconsistently between requests, count the rows for that email BEFORE anything else; two rows explains almost every otherwise-inexplicable symptom, because subsequent lookups pick one of them arbitrarily.

structured_data.symptom: registration is failing for one customer but not others
structured_data.refuse_the_framing: there is no registration function; registration is a side effect of verifying a sign-in code
four_faults: the code never arrived -- messaging or suppression
the code arrived and verification failed -- expiry, mismatch, or rate limit
verification succeeded but no customer row appeared
the account exists and a later step refuses on an incomplete profile -- correct behaviour, returns the missing list
triage_order: does an authentication user exist for that email
check verification records and the suppression list
structured_data.why_one_user: code paths do not discriminate between users; data does -- suppression, a stale verification record, a consumed rate limit, an unexpected row state, case or whitespace differences, a phone-only attempt
structured_data.structural_defect: the customer email column has no unique index, so creation is update-then-insert-if-none; two racing verifications can both insert, producing two rows for one identity
structured_data.first_query: count customer rows for that email -- two rows explains almost every inconsistent symptom

title: Nothing has run on a timer: the heartbeat is the first and only thing to check
content:
Symptom shapes that are all the same fault: no digest went out, no backup happened, the weekly report is missing, queued messages are not draining, metering has stopped. When MORE THAN ONE of those is true at once, stop investigating them individually -- they are all ticks inside one function driven by one external clock, and simultaneous failure means the clock, not the features.

Check the heartbeat by its EFFECTS, not by its configuration. A cron entry existing is a claim. What you want is evidence that the function actually ran within the last interval: the most recent row any of its ticks would have written, or the most recent run record for it. If the newest evidence is older than the interval by a meaningful multiple, the clock has stopped and everything else is downstream.

The causes, in likelihood order. The hosting platform did not fire the schedule. The route in front of the function returned an error before reaching it. The bearer secret in front of the route stopped matching. The function itself is failing early, before any tick -- note that the individual ticks each swallow their own errors, so a failure BEFORE the tick loop behaves very differently from a failure inside it. And a deploy that changed the route or the function.

If only ONE behaviour has stopped while the others continue, it is the opposite conclusion: the clock is fine and that tick is failing silently, which it is designed to do so that it cannot take the others down. In that case the investigation is entirely inside that tick and the heartbeat is irrelevant.

WHAT WILL MISLEAD YOU. Do not look at the database scheduler. It has one inactive job and runs nothing. Its run history still contains tens of thousands of successful entries from before the jobs were deleted, so a query counting recent runs will report a busy and healthy scheduler that does not exist. That number is history, not activity.

structured_data.symptom: one or more timed behaviours have stopped
structured_data.key_discriminator: MORE THAN ONE stopped at once means the clock; exactly one stopped means that tick, which swallows its own errors by design
structured_data.check_by: effects and their timestamps -- the newest row a tick would have written, or the newest run record -- never the cron configuration
causes_in_order: the hosting platform did not fire the schedule
the route in front returned an error before reaching the function
the bearer secret in front of the route stopped matching
the function failing early, before the tick loop
a deploy that changed the route or the function
structured_data.misleading: the database scheduler has one inactive job and runs nothing, but its run history holds tens of thousands of successful entries from before the deletion -- counting recent runs reports a healthy scheduler that does not exist

title: A successful status code carrying a failed result, and why status-only monitoring misses it
content:
The most expensive endpoint failure in this estate is not a five-hundred. It is a two-hundred whose body says the work did not happen. One function returned an explicit not-ok result at a successful status FOR WEEKS while every status-based monitor showed it healthy.

Why it happens by design rather than by accident: handlers catch their own errors so that one bad request does not take down a worker, and having caught, they must return something. Returning a successful status with a descriptive body is a reasonable choice for a caller that inspects results, and a catastrophic one for a monitor that inspects status codes.

THE RULE THAT FOLLOWS AND IT IS ABSOLUTE HERE: assert on a two-hundred AND on a non-zero effect. Never on the status alone. Every verification, every probe and every monitor must name the effect it expects -- a row written, a count increased, a field changed, a message queued -- and check that the effect occurred. A check that only reads the status is measuring the transport, not the work, which is an instrument pointed at the wrong subject.

How to find existing instances rather than waiting for one to hurt. Look for handlers with a broad catch that returns a successful status, and for any monitor whose assertion is a status code with no accompanying effect. Then, for each, construct the input that makes the work fail, send it, and observe what the monitor says. If it stays green, you have found one.

The same shape appears one level down: a routine that catches its own exception and returns a result object rather than raising. The caller sees success. The effect did not occur. Search for exception handling that swallows and returns, and treat each as a candidate.

structured_data.symptom: a successful status code whose body reports the work did not happen
structured_data.incident: a function returned an explicit not-ok result at a successful status for weeks while status monitors read healthy
structured_data.cause: handlers catch to stay available and must then return something; a descriptive body at a successful status is reasonable for callers and catastrophic for status monitors
structured_data.absolute_rule: assert on the status AND on a non-zero effect -- a row written, a count increased, a field changed, a message queued
structured_data.finding_instances: look for broad catches returning success, and for monitors asserting only a status; then send the input that makes the work fail and see whether the monitor stays green
structured_data.one_level_down: a routine that catches its own exception and returns a result object rather than raising produces the same blindness

title: An idempotency key collides against a previously failed row
content:
Symptom: a retry that should succeed is refused, and the refusal names a uniqueness violation on an idempotency key. It looks like the operation already happened. It did not.

The mechanism, and it is a genuinely easy mistake to make. The key column is unique, so a second attempt with the same key cannot insert. The guard written in front of it typically checks whether an operation with that key is already in progress or complete, and excludes only the LIVE statuses when it looks. A row left behind by a previous FAILED attempt is not in a live status, so the guard sees nothing, decides it is safe to proceed, and then the insert hits the unique index anyway.

So the failure presents as a contradiction: the pre-check says nothing exists, and the write says something does. That contradiction is the fingerprint. When you see a guard pass and a uniqueness violation follow, look for a status filter in the guard that does not cover every status the column can hold.

The fix is not to widen the unique constraint and not to remove it. It is to make the guard's status filter total: it must consider every state a prior attempt can leave behind, including failed, cancelled and abandoned, and then decide deliberately what to do with each -- reuse the row, or generate a new key, or refuse with a message that says which prior attempt is in the way.

The general lesson beyond this specific column: any pre-check whose filter is narrower than the constraint it is protecting will eventually disagree with that constraint, and the disagreement always surfaces at the worst moment, on a retry, when someone is already waiting.

structured_data.symptom: a retry refused by a uniqueness violation on an idempotency key, after a pre-check that found nothing
structured_data.mechanism: the key column is unique; the guard excludes only live statuses, so a previously failed row is invisible to the guard but still occupies the key
structured_data.fingerprint: a guard that passes followed by a uniqueness violation
structured_data.right_fix: make the guard's status filter total -- consider every state a prior attempt can leave, including failed, cancelled and abandoned, and decide deliberately for each
structured_data.general_lesson: a pre-check narrower than the constraint it protects will eventually disagree with it, and the disagreement surfaces on a retry

title: A routine in production does not match the file in the repository
content:
Symptom: behaviour that does not match the code you are reading. The endpoint does something the source says it should not, or a fix that was definitely applied appears not to have taken.

The first thing to know is what it CANNOT be. There is no pipeline that applies SQL. Nothing deploys a routine automatically on a push or a merge. So this is never a failed deployment, because there was no deployment. That eliminates the whole class of investigation people usually start with.

The actual causes, in order of frequency. The apply was never run -- the file was written, committed, reviewed and merged, and the step that puts it in the database is a separate manual action that somebody has to take. Or it was applied and then something LATER replaced the routine: another file defining the same routine applied after it, which is the reason apply ORDER decides ownership rather than commit time. Or two files define the same routine and the loser is the one you are reading.

How to settle it rather than argue about it: read the definition back out of the database and compare it to the file, byte for byte. That read-back is the definition of deployed in this estate -- not a successful command, not a green check, the definition matching. Then, if they differ, search the repository for every file defining that routine, because the presence of a second one is the answer.

The historical trap worth avoiding: an earlier check resolved which file owned a routine by git commit time and certified the wrong body. Commit time does not decide; apply order does. A file committed later can have been applied earlier, and the database holds whatever was applied last.

For edge functions the equivalent question is different, because they DO deploy on a push, filtered to changed paths, with promotion only from the main branch. A function whose files did not change will not redeploy on a push at all, which is exactly when a manual dispatch is the right tool.

structured_data.symptom: production behaviour does not match the source file
structured_data.cannot_be: a failed SQL deploy -- no pipeline applies SQL, so there was no deploy
causes_in_order: the apply was never run; applying is a separate manual action
it was applied and a later file defining the same routine replaced it
two files define the same routine and you are reading the loser
structured_data.settle_it: read the definition back out of the database and compare it to the file; the read-back match IS the definition of deployed
structured_data.then: search the repository for every file defining that routine
structured_data.historical_trap: an earlier check resolved ownership by git commit time and certified the wrong body; apply order decides, not commit time
structured_data.edge_functions_differ: they deploy on push filtered to changed paths, promotion only from main; a function whose files did not change needs a manual dispatch

title: A revoke that changed nothing, because the grant was held through PUBLIC
content:
Symptom: a permission was revoked, the command succeeded, and the role can still do the thing. Nothing errored and nothing changed.

The mechanism: revoking a privilege from a specific role is a silent no-op when that role does not hold the privilege directly but inherits it through PUBLIC. The command reports success because there was nothing to revoke from that role -- which is true, and completely misleading. The privilege is still there, held collectively.

Where it bites hardest: a newly CREATEd function is granted execute to PUBLIC automatically. So every new privileged routine is executable by everyone until somebody explicitly revokes from PUBLIC, and revoking from the anonymous role instead succeeds while leaving it wide open. This is the single most common way a privileged routine ends up reachable.

The rule: revoke from PUBLIC first, then from named roles if you want belt and braces. And CREATE OR REPLACE preserves the existing access list, so replacing a routine does not reopen it and does not need a second revoke -- which means the revoke belongs in the migration that CREATES, and adding one to a replacement is harmless but unnecessary.

How to verify rather than assume, and this is the only acceptable form of confirmation: after revoking, ASK whether the role can still execute, using the privilege-checking function, rather than reading the command's success. The estate keeps a check for exactly this on the anonymous role and treats a skipped run as a failure rather than a pass, which is the right posture -- a security check that could not run has told you nothing, and reading it as clean is how a hole survives an audit.

The general form, worth carrying to every permission question: a command's success reports what the command did, never what the resulting state is. Ask the state.

structured_data.symptom: a revoke succeeded and the role can still do the thing
structured_data.mechanism: revoking from a named role is a silent no-op when the privilege is held through PUBLIC
structured_data.worst_case: a newly CREATEd function is granted execute to PUBLIC automatically, so revoking from the anonymous role alone leaves it open
structured_data.rule: revoke from PUBLIC first, then named roles
structured_data.create_or_replace: preserves the access list, so a replacement does not reopen and needs no second revoke; the revoke belongs with the CREATE
structured_data.verification: ask whether the role can still execute using the privilege-checking function, never read the command's success
structured_data.estate_posture: the anonymous-role check treats a SKIP as a failure, because a check that could not run has told you nothing
structured_data.general_form: a command's success reports what it did, never what the resulting state is

title: Counts match and behaviour does not: signature parity is not behaviour parity
content:
Symptom: a comparison says two things are identical and they behave differently. The specific instance that cost time here was a count of functions -- eight hundred and thirty-seven on each side, therefore equal, therefore fine. Six triggers were missing. Functions and triggers are different objects, and counting one said nothing about the other.

The general shape: an equality check compares a PROJECTION of two systems, and the projection omits the thing that differs. Names match while bodies differ. Bodies match while grants differ. Grants match while triggers differ. Row counts match while the rows differ. Every one of those comparisons is real, correct, and insufficient on its own, and each produces a confident equal.

So the discipline when reading any parity or drift result: say what the comparison compared, and then say what it did not. Not as a caveat but as part of the result. A comparison of function signatures has told you about function signatures. If somebody asks whether the two systems agree, that is a broader question than the check answered, and answering the broader question from the narrower check is the same defect as a bounded measurement producing an unbounded claim.

What to do when you need real confidence: compare the thing that actually determines behaviour, which is usually the full definition rather than the identity, and compare the SET of objects rather than the count of them -- a set difference finds a missing item and a swapped pair, while a count finds neither. Two systems can hold different objects in equal numbers indefinitely.

And when a comparison finds no differences, apply the other lens before relaxing: prove that both sides were actually read. A comparison against something unreachable also finds no differences.

structured_data.symptom: an equality check says identical and the systems behave differently
structured_data.incident: 837 functions on each side read as parity while six triggers were missing -- different object classes
structured_data.general_shape: the comparison compares a projection and the projection omits what differs
structured_data.discipline: state what the comparison compared AND what it did not, as part of the result
for_real_confidence: compare full definitions rather than identities
compare the SET of objects rather than the count -- a set difference finds a missing item and a swapped pair, a count finds neither
structured_data.companion_lens: when a comparison finds no differences, prove both sides were actually read

title: Everything is slow at once versus one thing is slow: the split that decides the whole investigation
content:
The first question on any latency complaint, before any measurement, is whether it is broad or narrow, because the two have almost no diagnostic overlap and starting on the wrong branch wastes the session.

BROAD -- many unrelated operations slower at the same time -- points at a shared resource. In this estate that means the database first: a long-running statement holding locks, a table whose statistics have gone stale enough to flip a plan, a connection pool exhausted by something that opened connections and did not return them, or an autovacuum-starved table where dead rows have accumulated. It can also mean the region or the platform, which is diagnosed by checking whether anything is fast, and is confirmed from outside rather than from inside.

NARROW -- one operation slower while everything else is normal -- points at that operation's own path. A plan that changed for one query. A loop that grew with the data. A call to a third party that is now slower and is being awaited. A retry with a backoff that is now being reached. A cache that is missing when it used to hit.

That last one is the highest-prior-probability cause in this estate right now, and it is worth checking early on any narrow slowness: caching is present in the design and, where it has been measured, not actually storing anything. A path designed around a cache that never hits does the expensive work every single time, and it will look like gradual degradation as data grows rather than like a defect, because nothing ever errors.

The measurement that separates broad from narrow without guessing: take two unrelated operations, time both, and compare each against its own history. If both moved, it is shared. If one moved, it is that one. Timing a single operation and comparing it to a feeling is not a measurement and produces the wrong branch about half the time.

structured_data.first_question: broad or narrow, before any measurement
broad_causes: a connection pool exhausted by leaked connections
dead rows accumulating on a vacuum-starved table
the region or platform, confirmed from outside
narrow_causes: a plan that changed for one query
a loop that grew with the data
a slower third party being awaited
a retry backoff now being reached
a cache missing where it used to hit
structured_data.highest_prior_here: a cache that is present in the design and stores nothing, so the expensive work happens every time and it looks like gradual degradation because nothing errors
structured_data.separating_measurement: time two unrelated operations and compare each against its own history; both moved means shared, one moved means that one

title: The website looks fine and nothing works: reads are cached and writes are not
content:
Symptom: the site loads, pages render, navigation works, and every action fails or silently does nothing. Or the inverse and equally confusing: a customer reports seeing stale information while the database plainly holds the new value.

The mechanism is that reads and writes take different paths with different failure modes. A rendered page can be served from a cache or from a build artefact and will keep serving long after the data layer behind it has become unreachable. So availability of the site is not evidence of availability of anything else, and an uptime check that fetches a page is checking that the page can be fetched.

What that means for monitoring: a synthetic check must exercise a WRITE path, not a read path, or it will report health throughout a total write outage. The write it exercises has to be one that is safe to perform repeatedly and leaves nothing behind -- which is what the aborted-transaction pattern is for on the database side, and what a designated no-op endpoint is for on the application side.

For the stale-data direction, the questions in order: is the value actually in the database; if so, is the reader reading the right row -- remember that a duplicate row for one identity makes subsequent lookups pick arbitrarily; if so, is the response cached; and only then, is the browser holding it. Going straight to the browser is the common mistake and it is the last link in the chain, not the first.

And the portal-specific trap that has been reported as a product bug and was not one: signing a portal session in by hand requires setting THREE storage keys, not the obvious two, because the client library persists its own session under a custom key. Set only two and the next page load silently restores the PREVIOUS account from the third. That looks exactly like an account-mixup defect. Before investigating a session or identity anomaly, establish whether the session was created through the real screens or by hand.

structured_data.symptom_a: the site renders and every action fails
structured_data.symptom_b: stale data shown while the database holds the new value
structured_data.mechanism: reads and writes take different paths; a page can serve from cache or a build artefact long after the data layer is unreachable
structured_data.monitoring_rule: a synthetic check must exercise a WRITE path, or it reports health throughout a total write outage
structured_data.safe_write: the aborted-transaction pattern on the database side, a designated no-op endpoint on the application side
stale_data_order: is the value in the database

title: The alert fired and nobody heard it, or fired constantly and everybody stopped listening
content:
Two failure modes of the alerting system itself, and a monitoring seat that does not audit its own alerting is monitoring nothing.

SILENCE. An alert exists, its condition became true, and no message arrived. The causes here, in order: the kind was not registered, so it was routed to a task instead of emailed and the only trace is a routed alert row -- see the record on the mail gate, because this outcome is invisible unless you know to look for it. Or the alert is deduplicated against a marker that was set and never cleared, so the first occurrence suppressed every subsequent one indefinitely. Or the sending path is the same queued path that depends on the heartbeat, so a stopped clock silences alerts as well as everything else -- which is the worst version, because the outage suppresses its own notification.

That last one deserves stating plainly: an alerting path that shares infrastructure with the thing it monitors cannot report that infrastructure failing. Any alert about the scheduler must not travel via the scheduler. Check what an alert's delivery depends on before trusting it to tell you about a dependency.

NOISE. An alert fires continuously, the channel is muted in practice, and every other alert on it is now invisible too. The causes: a threshold set against an assumption that has changed; a condition that fires on the healthy state; a per-occurrence alert on something that occurs constantly; and dedupe that is absent or keyed too specifically, so a thousand instances of one fault produce a thousand messages.

The audit that catches both, and it is worth doing on a schedule rather than after an incident: for every alert, when did it last fire, and does the answer make sense. Never is suspicious. Constantly is suspicious. Both are more informative than the alert's definition, which describes intent.

structured_data.failure_a: silence -- the condition became true and no message arrived
silence_causes: the kind was not registered, so it routed to a task; the only trace is a routed alert row
dedupe against a marker that was set and never cleared
the sending path depends on the heartbeat, so a stopped clock silences alerts too
structured_data.worst_version: an alerting path sharing infrastructure with the thing it monitors cannot report that infrastructure failing; an alert about the scheduler must not travel via the scheduler
structured_data.failure_b: noise -- continuous firing, the channel muted in practice, every other alert now invisible

a condition that fires on the healthy state
a per-occurrence alert on something constant

title: A cost spike is usually a loop, and out-of-credit looks exactly like a model refusing
content:
Two cost-shaped incidents that present as something else entirely.

A SPIKE IS ALMOST NEVER DEMAND. Where the company is pre-launch, a sudden rise in provider spend is not customers arriving. The realistic causes are a retry loop with no ceiling, a recursive or re-entrant call path, a cache that stopped hitting so every request does full work, a batch job that lost its bound and is reprocessing everything each run, or an automated caller stuck in a tight cycle. Each of those is a defect that happens to be denominated in money, and the remedy is a bound rather than a budget.

So the first query on a spend anomaly is not how much, it is how many calls and from where, grouped by caller and by hour. A count that has gone up by orders of magnitude while the subject count stayed flat is a loop, and the shape of the hourly distribution usually names it -- a loop is flat and relentless, real demand is not.

OUT OF CREDIT LOOKS LIKE JUDGEMENT. When a provider account is exhausted, the failure that comes back can be indistinguishable from the model declining, returning empty, or producing a degraded answer, and the system may fall back to a deterministic path that looks like a deliberate design choice. Whole sessions have been spent debugging reasoning quality when the actual condition was a balance. Before investigating output quality, check the account balance and the meter -- there is a metering tick that records readings precisely so this question has an answer that is not a guess.

The related trap: the tier is the bill, not the prompt. Spend follows which model was selected and how many tokens crossed the wire, not how the request was worded. Optimising prompt text while an expensive model is being selected for a cheap task treats the symptom.

spike_causes: a retry loop with no ceiling
a recursive or re-entrant call path
a batch job that lost its bound
an automated caller in a tight cycle
structured_data.framing: a spike pre-launch is a defect denominated in money; the remedy is a bound, not a budget
structured_data.first_query: how many calls and from where, grouped by caller and hour -- not how much
structured_data.fingerprint: call count up by orders of magnitude with subject count flat; a loop is flat and relentless, demand is not
structured_data.out_of_credit: an exhausted account is indistinguishable from a model declining, returning empty, or degrading, and a deterministic fallback looks like a design choice
structured_data.before_debugging_quality: check the balance and the meter; a metering tick records readings so this is not a guess
structured_data.tier_trap: the tier is the bill, not the prompt -- spend follows model selection and token volume, not wording

title: Two rows for one identity, and every symptom it causes downstream
content:
Symptom family: a user sees different data on different requests; an update appears to work and then reverts; a lookup returns a record that is missing fields another part of the system definitely wrote; a customer says they registered and a search says they did not, then says they did.

All of those are one cause. Two rows exist for one identity, and different code paths select different ones, arbitrarily, because nothing orders the choice.

How it happens without anyone writing a bug. The identifying column carries no unique index, so the database will not prevent it. The creation path is therefore an update-by-identifier followed by an insert if nothing was updated, which is correct in sequence and unsafe under concurrency: two requests can both find nothing to update and both insert. Any retry, any double-submit, any two devices verifying at once, any duplicate webhook delivery can do it.

Why it is so hard to see from a bug report: the symptoms are inconsistent by construction, which reads as flakiness, which gets attributed to caching or to the network. The reporter cannot reproduce it reliably because reproduction depends on which row a given path happened to pick.

THE FIRST QUERY on any inconsistent single-user symptom is therefore a count of rows for that identity. It is one statement, it costs nothing, and it either explains everything or eliminates a whole class of theory. Do it before reading any code.

The durable fix is a unique index, which turns the race into a constraint violation the creation path can catch and handle by re-reading. Adding one requires resolving the duplicates that already exist, which is why it is usually deferred and why the condition persists. The remediation of existing duplicates is a data decision about which row is authoritative and what happens to what is attached to the other -- that is not something to guess at during an incident.

symptoms: an update that works then reverts
a record missing fields another path wrote
a user found, then not found, then found
structured_data.single_cause: two rows for one identity; different paths select different ones arbitrarily
structured_data.mechanism: no unique index on the identifying column, so creation is update-then-insert-if-none, which is unsafe under concurrency
structured_data.why_hard_to_see: symptoms are inconsistent by construction, read as flakiness, and get attributed to caching or the network
structured_data.first_query: count rows for that identity -- one statement, before reading any code
structured_data.durable_fix: a unique index, which converts the race into a catchable constraint violation
structured_data.blocker_on_the_fix: existing duplicates must be resolved first, which is a data decision about authority and attachments, not an incident-time guess

title: A third party is fine and we are still broken: the four places a working integration fails
content:
Symptom: the provider's status page is green, a direct call from a terminal works, and the feature is still broken. The integration is not down; something between it and us is.

The four places, and they are checked in this order because each is cheaper than the next.

CREDENTIAL. The key we hold is not the key that works. It expired, it was rotated on their side, it is the wrong environment's key, or it is scoped to permissions that no longer include what we ask for. This is first because it is the most common and the easiest to confirm: make the same call with the credential the system actually holds, not with one from a terminal or a password manager. Those are frequently different, and the difference is the whole bug.

SHAPE. Their contract changed, or ours drifted. A field became required, a value became an enum, a response gained a level of nesting. The call succeeds at the transport level and fails at the semantic level, which is the two-hundred-with-a-failed-body pattern again.

RETURN PATH. They accepted the work and told us about it, and we did not hear -- a webhook endpoint that is unreachable, a signature that no longer verifies, a handler that errors after accepting, or a retry window that expired while we were deploying. The work HAPPENED. Only the record of it is missing, which is the two-facts pattern.

OUR SIDE OF THE CALL. Timeouts too short for their current latency, a bounded retry that now always exhausts, a rate limit we are hitting, or an outbound path blocked by something in front of us.

The discipline throughout: reproduce with what the system holds and from where the system calls. A successful call made by a human with a human's credentials from a human's machine proves that a call can succeed, which was never in question.

structured_data.symptom: the provider is green, a manual call works, the feature is broken

four_places_in_order.detail: expired, rotated on their side, wrong environment, or scope narrowed
four_places_in_order.confirm: make the call with the credential the SYSTEM holds, not one from a terminal or password manager

four_places_in_order.detail: their contract changed or ours drifted; succeeds at transport, fails at semantics
unreachable webhook, signature no longer verifying, handler erroring after acceptance, retry window expired during a deploy -- the work happened, the record is missing
timeouts too short, a bounded retry always exhausting, a rate limit, an outbound block

structured_data.discipline: reproduce with what the system holds and from where the system calls; a human's successful call proves only that a call can succeed
